releasesInRange.name: pnpm 12.5
releasesInRange.body:
pnpm 12.5.0 makes Python a first-class ecosystem, accepts Package URLs in `pnpm add`, names whole platforms in `supportedArchitectures`, and gives tasks machine-wide concurrency limits. It also fixes an install that could reuse one package's downloaded tarball for another.

## Minor Changes

### Installing packages

- `pnpm add` accepts a [Package URL](https://github.com/package-url/purl-spec) in place of a package name. `pnpm add pkg:npm/express@4.18.2` saves `express` to `package.json`. `pnpm add pkg:cargo/serde@1.0.188` saves `serde` to `Cargo.toml`. `pnpm add pkg:pypi/requests@2.31.0` saves `requests` to `pyproject.toml`. `pkg` is now a reserved specifier prefix, whatever case it is written in, so a named registry can no longer be called `pkg`.

- A `registries` entry can now name the ecosystem it serves.

  ```yaml
  registries:
    https://internal.example/simple/:
      ecosystem: pypi
    https://pypi.org/simple/:
      ecosystem: pypi
    https://index.crates.io/:
      ecosystem: cargo
  ```

  `ecosystem` accepts `npm`, `cargo` and `pypi`. An entry that does not name one serves npm, as every entry did before.

  An ecosystem with several indexes searches them in the order they are declared. The first index that has a package supplies it, so the one declared last answers what none before it had.

  A `registries` entry may not carry credentials. pnpm reads them from `.npmrc`, matched by origin, for a PyPI index as for every other package source.

### Configuring pnpm

- `supportedArchitectures` now accepts a list of platforms, in place of the `os`, `cpu` and `libc` axes.

  ```yaml
  supportedArchitectures:
    - linux-x64
    - darwin-arm64
    - win32-x64
  ```

  An install prepares for the platforms the list names, and for those only. A platform reads as `<os>-<cpu>`, with a C library on Linux, as in `linux-x64-musl` or `linux-x64-manylinux_2_28`. The Rust target triple of the same machine is accepted too, so `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` names the platform `linux-x64` names. A Linux platform that names no C library is the glibc platform. `current` is the platform the install runs on.

  The `os`, `cpu` and `libc` mapping keeps working and keeps its meaning.

- Added concurrency groups for tasks. A task in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` can name a `concurrencyGroup`. The new `concurrencyGroups` setting gives each group a limit. At most that many tasks of the group run at once on the machine, counted across every pnpm process, `pnpm pipeline` included. A task past the limit waits for a running one to finish. A script that calls `pnpm run` for a task of the same group runs under the slot its parent holds.

  ```yaml
  tasks:
    test:rust:
      concurrencyGroup: cargo
  concurrencyGroups:
    cargo: 2
  ```

- `tools` names the programs pnpm downloads, and `mirror` says where each one comes from.

  ```yaml
  tools:
    node:
      mirror: https://mirror.example.com/node/download
      channels:
        nightly: https://nightly.example.com/
    
…(truncated)

releasesInRange.name: pnpm 12.5.1
releasesInRange.body: ## Patch Changes - pnpm now reports an unknown task setting in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and carries on. It used to refuse to start, so a project could not use a task setting that only the pnpm version its `packageManager` pins reads. The setting is still an error when the running pnpm is that pinned version. - Python interpreter installation now retries historical release metadata requests. It caches the release list for up to 24 hours and refreshes it once after a lookup miss. When a release omits the current platform, the search samples at most eight other releases before reporting that the lookup is inconclusive. - Python `registries` entries now route packages by exact names or trailing-prefix patterns in `packages`. Registry declaration order no longer affects resolution. A matched package resolves exclusively from its assigned registry, including transitive and build dependencies. Use `packages: ["*"]` to declare the default index. - `pnpm install` no longer fails with "Too many levels of symbolic links" when a Cargo configuration file above the workspace is a symlink, such as a `~/.cargo/config.toml` linked from a dotfiles repository. - `pnpm install` now returns "Already up to date" in a workspace where `dedupeDirectDeps` left a project without a `node_modules` directory of its own. Such a project forced a full install on every run. - `pnpm install` no longer refuses the repeat-install fast path just because a changed `pnpm-lock.yaml` is 16 MiB or larger. Such a lockfile forced a full install on the run after every change. ## Platinum Sponsors

releasesInRange.name: pnpm 11.27.1
releasesInRange.body:
## Patch Changes

* `pn`, `pnpx`, and `pnx` now run the pnpm installed alongside them. They used to look pnpm up on `PATH`. That failed when the directory holding them was not on `PATH`, and it silently handed the call to an unrelated pnpm when one came first there [#14803](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/14803).

* The `@zkochan/cmd-shim` package is now available as `@pnpm/bins.cmd-shim`.

* `pnpm cache list-registries` now prints the registry URL, matching `pnpm cache view`. It printed `https%3A+registry.npmjs.org` before and prints `https://registry.npmjs.org/` now [#15046](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/15046).

* `pnpm deploy` no longer installs the dependencies of the workspace root project into the deploy directory [#6437](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/6437).

* Install warnings no longer carry the text of a package's deprecation notice. The warning names the deprecated package and version, and the `pnpm:deprecation` event no longer carries the notice either. `pnpm view` still shows it on request.

  A deprecation warning now names the newest version of the package that is not deprecated, and says when reaching it means widening the range you declared:

  ```
  WARN  deprecated foo@1.0.0. 2.3.1 is not deprecated, outside the range you declared.
  ```

  pnpm works this out from the metadata it already fetched, so it costs no extra request. An install that reuses the lockfile without fetching metadata names no version.

  pnpm strips control characters from the package name and version in a deprecation warning, and from the notice `pnpm outdated --long` prints.

  The text sanitizer now also strips the Unicode line and paragraph separators U+2028 and U+2029.

* `pnpm exec <command>` and `pnpm <command>` run from a subdirectory of a project now find the executables installed in the project's `node_modules/.bin`. The command still runs in the subdirectory. `PNPM_PACKAGE_NAME` names the project [#5068](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/5068).

* `pnpm exec` and `pnpm dlx` now wait for the command to finish shutting down after `Ctrl+C`. A signal sent to pnpm alone now reaches the command, the way it does with `pnpm run`. pnpm used to exit on the interrupt and terminate the command while it was still shutting down [#7374](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/7374).

* Warnings about ignored environment variables in project `.npmrc` credentials now link to the npmrc documentation [pnpm/pnpm#15051](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/15051).

* `pnpm audit --interactive --fix=update` no longer opens a second prompt for selecting dependencies to update [#14927](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/14927).

* Fixed `pnpm dedupe` requiring a second pass after bumping a direct dependency in `package.json` [pnpm/pnpm#14987](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/14987).

* `pnpm deploy` now writes plain versions for registry dependencies with peer dependencies in the deployed `package.json`. The deployed lockfile retains the resolved peer b
…(truncated)

releasesInRange.name: pnpm 12.6
releasesInRange.body:
pnpm 12.6.0 ships with automatic dependency deduplication, relocatable node_modules, package.yaml manifest editing, and --save-types support.

### Minor Changes

- `autoDedupe` deduplicates compatible dependency versions during installation [#7258](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/7258). Enable it in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or use `pnpm install --auto-dedupe` or `pnpm add --auto-dedupe`. Frozen installs leave the lockfile unchanged.

- `pnpm install`, `pnpm run`, and `pnpm exec` on macOS and Linux now reuse a `node_modules` directory and bin shims that moved or were copied together with their project [#6937](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/6937). The first command after the move checks the tree and records its new location, so project commands in `node_modules/.bin` keep working.

- `pnpm add --save-types` saves available `@types/*` packages in `devDependencies` alongside registry dependencies [#3868](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/3868). Packages that declare bundled TypeScript types are skipped. Set `saveTypes: true` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` to enable this by default.

- `package.yaml` manifests can now be updated by `pnpm add`, `pnpm update`, `pnpm remove`, `pnpm pkg`, `pnpm link`, `pnpm set-script`, and `pnpm version` [#2008](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/2008). Existing comments and key order are preserved.

- Catalog entries can now use the `file:` and `link:` protocols [#8642](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/8642). A relative path or bare path in an entry, such as `./tarballs/foo.tgz`, is measured from the directory holding `pnpm-workspace.yaml`.

- `pnpm tasks status` lists running and waiting tasks in each concurrency group, and waiting tasks now take available slots in arrival order with higher `priority` tasks going first [#15208](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/15208). If workspaces use different limits for the same group, a later task can take a free slot that earlier tasks cannot use. A package script named `tasks` takes precedence; use `pnpm pm tasks status` when that script exists.

- `pnpm cache prune` deletes registry metadata cache directories that this version of pnpm can no longer read [#15046](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/15046). `pnpm cache prune --dry-run` lists what it would delete without removing anything.

- `macosBackup.excludeModulesDir` and `macosBackup.excludeStoreDir` on macOS can now exclude newly created modules, virtual-store, and package-store directories from Time Machine [#6440](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/6440). Set either to `true` in global configuration or using the `PNPM_CONFIG_MACOS_BACKUP_EXCLUDE_MODULES_DIR` and `PNPM_CONFIG_MACOS_BACKUP_EXCLUDE_STORE_DIR` environment variables.

- `pnpm add --tilde` is now an alias for `--save-prefix=~` [#12863](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/12863). The Yarn `-T` shorthand is not supported.

- `progress` setting and `--no-progress` option now turn off dependency and download progress lines [#14065](https://github.com/pnpm
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(python-installer): scope Python projects by the workspace selection
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes item 12 of pnpm/pnpm#14945: `--filter` was ignored by the Python participant, so every Python project in the workspace was resolved, locked and materialized whatever the selection asked for, and `pnpm add --filter … pypi:…` refused to run at all.

The Python participant now reads every discovered manifest once and prepares only the selected projects:

- A Python project that shares a directory with an npm workspace project follows that project's selection. The npm project's name is what the workspace knows that directory by.
- A Python project in a directory of its own runs through the same selector engine the npm side uses, matched against the distribution it declares, its path, and the `[tool.uv.sources]` edges to its siblings (so `--filter app...` reaches them).
- The projects the selection leaves out are still parsed: a selected project installs the siblings it declares a source for, so what those declare belongs to its resolution. They just get no environment or `pylock.toml` of their own.

`--fail-if-no-match` is no longer decided while resolving the npm projects. The install waits until the Python selection is known, so a selector that names only a Python project counts as a match, and a workspace whose projects are all Python is not reported as holding no project at all.

prs.title: feat(python): install a release from its source distribution
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Item 5 of pnpm/pnpm#14945, "No source distributions". Related to pnpm/pnpm#14945 — this covers that one item and none of the others.

Two of the eight repositories surveyed in that issue depend on a distribution that publishes no wheel at all: sentry needs `python-u2flib-server` (15 source distributions, 0 wheels on PyPI) and marimo needs `lzstring` (wheels stop at 1.0.3). Both failed with `Python project 0 depends on python-u2flib-server ∅`, which said neither that the distribution exists nor that it ships only an sdist.

What this changes:

- A release whose wheels the target accepts none of is offered as the source distribution the index serves beside it. Source candidates rank after every wheel, so a wheel always wins and the archive is downloaded only where nothing else installs. `.tar.gz` and `.zip` are read.
- The archive goes through pnpm's shared artifact pipeline (`ArchiveStoreProjection::RawArchive`), so it gets the SHA-256 check, retries, store dedup and offline replay the wheel path already has. Its files are copied out of the CAS into a temporary tree before the backend runs, so a build writes beside its own sources and not into shared store content.
- The archive is accepted only over HTTP(S), checked at the lockfile boundary and again before any build. The store fetches a `file:` URL from the filesystem, and a `pylock.toml` is untrusted input, so without that check a lockfile could have pnpm read an archive off this machine and run its build backen
…(truncated)

prs.title: feat(run): task concurrency groups with machine-wide limits
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds task concurrency groups to pnpm v12. A task in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` names a `concurrencyGroup`, and the new `concurrencyGroups` setting gives each group a limit. At most that many tasks of the group run at once on the machine, counted across every pnpm process: `pnpm run`, the script shortcuts, and the tasks of a `pnpm pipeline`, in every worktree that shares the pool. A task past the limit waits and prints who holds the slots.

```yaml
tasks:
  test:rust:
    concurrencyGroup: cargo
concurrencyGroups:
  cargo: 2
```

Motivation: several agents working in separate worktrees of this repository each build the CLI or run the Rust suite at the same time, and the machine runs out of memory. A named group holds the heavy scripts to a limit while the light ones (lint, a small unit test run) keep running.

Design:

- **Slots are advisory file locks.** A group's pool is `N` files under `<stateDir>/run-slots/<group>/`; a task holds an exclusive lock on one through `File::try_lock` for every stage of its script. The OS releases the lock when the holder ends, however it ends, so there is no stale-slot cleanup and no Windows special case beyond `LockFileEx`.
- **One hook point.** `run_stages` takes the slot, so the single-project run, the recursive run, and the pipeline are all counted, and each project's task in a recursive run counts separately. `pnpm exec` names no task and is not gated.
- **Nested runs reuse the parent's slot.** A holder lists its group in `PNPM_HELD
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(package-manager): read the manifest of a tarball a resolver left without one
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15000.

`manifest` is optional in the `ResolveResult` a pnpmfile `resolvers` hook returns. pnpm 11 awaits the fetch and reads the bundled manifest when the resolver supplies none. pacquet had no equivalent, so `walk::fallback_manifest` synthesized an identity-only manifest, `extract_children` found no children, and the package installed alone — no dependencies, no `engines`, exit 0 and no warning. The repro in the issue leaves `debug@4.3.4` unable to `require('ms')`.

`PrefetchingResolver` already fetches an archive during resolution to learn an integrity the resolution does not carry. This widens that to the manifest: one read settles both, shared across every edge that resolves to the same content, and it warms the mem cache so the install pass reuses the extraction rather than downloading again.

The read now verifies the bytes against a pinned hash (`FetchTarballForResolution::expected_integrity`). Discovering an integrity has nothing to check against, but a resolution that already pins one is read here only for its manifest, and unchecked bytes would put a tampered archive in charge of the dependency walk. The native cache key carries the pinned hash as well as the URL, so a read that verifies is never served the bytes of one that could not.

`file:` and git-hosted tarballs keep their existing handling: the local and git resolvers already fill both fields for the shapes they own.

prs.title: feat(python): let a workspace share one environment between its members
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15015. Follows up on item 14 of pnpm/pnpm#14945.

A workspace root that declares `[tool.uv.workspace]` can now set `shared-environment = true` under `[tool.pnpm.python]`:

```toml
[tool.uv.workspace]
members = ["packages/*"]

[tool.pnpm.python]
shared-environment = true
```

`pnpm install` then resolves every member as one graph, the way uv resolves a workspace, into one `pylock.toml` and one `.venv` at the workspace root. Each project keeps an environment of its own by default, so a repository can share where its projects agree and stay independent where they do not, without splitting into separate workspaces.

What a shared environment means for the features the issue lists as open questions:

- **Extras and groups** stay a per-member selection (`[tool.pnpm.python]` in each member, or the workspace defaults). The environment holds the union.
- **`--filter`** selecting any member installs the whole shared environment. An environment holding only the selected members would leave the others unable to run.
- **The lockfile** records the members it answers for under `tool.pnpm.members` as paths relative to it, and its `requires-python` is the range every member accepts together. Adding or removing a member invalidates it. Which member each package belongs to is not recorded; PEP 751 has no importers concept, and nothing in pnpm reads such a mapping yet.
- **Conflicts.** Two members that require versions of one distribution that no offered release sat
…(truncated)

prs.title: feat(python-installer): keep environment generations in the store
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15014, the placement half of item 14 of pnpm/pnpm#14945.

Python environment generations move out of each project's `.pnpm/python-envs/` into the store, under `<store>/python-envs/<project>/`. The project keeps only `.venv`, an absolute link to the generation it currently runs. A repository with many Python projects therefore holds one link per project instead of a generation directory each, and nothing is written into a project's `.pnpm` any more.

What stays the same:

- Publication is still an atomic symlink rename in the project directory, and rollback still republishes the previous link. The generation is a `TempDir` in the store until publication retains it, so a failed sibling still discards it.
- A `.venv` that is a real directory, or a link to an environment pnpm did not make, is still refused rather than replaced.
- Every per-project guarantee: extras and groups, interpreter selection, `--filter` scoping.

What changes beyond placement:

- Upgrading: 12.4 published `.venv` as a link into the project's own `.pnpm/python-envs`. That location still counts as pnpm's when `.pnpm` and `.pnpm/python-envs` are real directories, which is all 12.4 ever published through, so the next install relinks `.venv` into the store and leaves the old directory in place, since a running program may still use it.

Follow-up to pnpm/pnpm#15019, which merged while its last review round was still being worked. Qodo's review summary there listed four items that never became inline threads; this carries their fixes. Related to pnpm/pnpm#15015.

prs.title: fix(tarball): key the tarball mem cache by expected integrity
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

The tarball `MemCache` named its slots by tarball URL and archive projection alone, and `IngestTarballToStore::run_with_mem_cache_inner` handed a `CacheValue::Available` to the caller without comparing the request's expected hash against the one the slot's bytes were verified with. Two resolutions naming the same URL but pinning different integrities shared one slot, and whichever got there second was served the other's bytes.

An archive's cache identity is now its URL, its expected hash, the network policy the fetch runs under and the archive projection, and every writer and reader agrees on it. The three gates that deduplicated by URL for the same reason move with it: `PrefetchingResolver`'s spawn gate, the pnpr client's `TarballPrefetcher`, and `ObservingResolver`'s frame dedup.

Git stages a hardlink like any other file and reports the tree clean afterwards:

## Summary

An `install` through the Node-API bindings (`@pnpm/napi`) never took a repeat-install short-circuit. prs.title: perf(cli/add): move the npm selectors into the plan instead of cloning them
prs.author: KSXGitHub
prs.body:
## Summary

`PackageSpecifierPlan::parse` took a `&[AddRequest]`, so every selector the npm add path reads as it was written was cloned on its way into the plan. It now takes the requests by value and moves each one.

The other arms are untouched. Cargo, Python and each purl type build a new selector out of the parsed components, so none of them ever needed to own what it was handed, and a purl still mints its request through `AddRequest::from_package_url`.

`IntoIterator` rather than a slice or a `Vec` because `parse` iterates once, front to back, and never indexes or asks for a length. The one production caller owns its vector and overwrites it on the next line, so `std::mem::take` hands it over at no cost, and the test call sites pass their array by value rather than by reference.

Allocations through `parse`, counted with a global allocator:

| `pnpm add …` | before | after |

## Summary

A `readPackage` hook that adds a dependency to one of your dependencies records
that dependency in `pnpm-lock.yaml`. Removing the hook did not take it back out:
it stayed locked, and every later install kept it. The same happened when the
hook was edited rather than removed. Closes pnpm/pnpm#3735.

## Summary

Installs running in different projects heal one global-virtual-store slot at the
same time, so one of them can inspect a file another has just unlinked. Windows
keeps such a file *delete-pending* until the last handle on it closes, and
answers `PermissionDenied` rather than `NotFound` for as long as that lasts.
Every inspection site treated anything but `NotFound` as fatal, so the losing

takes effect at once.

already reads it as an absent target.

budget for permission errors that can also mean a permanent ACL problem, and no
retrying at all off Windows. The new `symlink_metadata_with_retry` reuses it, so
a genuine permission problem still fails within a second and Unix still fails
immediately.

`file_matches_store_entry` is the one inspection left alone. It reports any
failure as a mismatch, so a delete-pending file is simply written again, which
is the healing path rather than an error.

prs.title: fix(resolving): omit etag validator on upgraded release age metadata
prs.author: Ayush442842q
prs.body:
## Summary

When `minimumReleaseAge` forces an abbreviated packument to be upgraded to the full document, the upgraded document is written into the **abbreviated** mirror slot (`pkgMirror`) so the next install finds `time` there and skips the upgrade fetch.

An `ETag` identifies one representation (RFC 9110). Writing the full document's `ETag` into the abbreviated slot makes the next abbreviated request (`Accept: application/vnd.npm.install-v1+json`) send `If-None-Match: "full-etag"`. A registry that keys `ETag`s per representation, such as npmjs.org, can never match that validator, so it answers `200 OK` with an abbreviated body, the `time` map is lost, and the upgrade runs again.

The upgrade reaches the mirror from two directions, and both now write no `ETag`:

- `persistUpgradedMeta` — a `304` validated the cached mirror and the upgrade replaced it with the full document.
- `persistFreshMeta` — a fresh abbreviated `200` on a cold cache triggered the upgrade.

The rationale lives on their common callee, `prepareJsonForDisk`, rather than above each call site.

**`modified` is deliberately kept.** It comes from the packument's own `time.modified`, a package-level fact both representations report identically, so it still describes the slot. The next abbreviated request therefore stays conditional through `If-Modified-Since` and can still be answered with a `304`. Without that, dropping the validator would leave every later abbreviated request unconditional.

prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Two findings arrived on pnpm/pnpm#15160 while it sat in the merge queue, and it
merged before either was answered. Both were right; this is them.

### A slot another installer finished repairing was rejected

Clearing a blocker happens in two steps: decide what stands in the way, then
remove it by path. Between them, the installer healing the same slot can clear
the blocker and create the directory the path needs. The removal then lands on
that directory and fails, `IsADirectory` on Unix and a refusal on Windows, so
the install gives up over a path that had become exactly what it was asking for.

pnpm/pnpm#15160 made this likelier rather than causing it: retrying the removal
widens the window between the two steps.

A failed removal is no longer read as a failed clearing when the path fits what
it was being cleared for. `dir_fits_at` and `file_fits_at` say what that means,
and they subsume the `NotFound` case that was special-cased before, since a path
with nothing at it fits either way. pnpm 11 gets the same through `dirFitsAt`.

Raised by Qodo at https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/15160#discussion_r4057019233.

### The changeset explained the mechanism

`AGENTS.md` asks a changeset to state what pnpm does now and leave design
rationale to the commit body. The second sentence described how Windows reports
a delete-pending file, so it is gone and the entry ends on the issue link.

After a full resolution, pnpm checks every convergence override (`"pkg@": "<version>"`) for staleness by resolving each of its collected declared ranges through the registry. ## Summary

`pnpm audit --fix=update` silently skipped vulnerable dependencies declared through an npm alias, such as `"myfoo": "npm:vulnerable-pkg@1.0.0"`.

Two problems in the vulnerability-update loop in `mutateModules` (`pnpm11/installing/deps-installer/src/install/index.ts`):

1. `semver.valid(dep.bareSpecifier)` rejects alias strings like `npm:vulnerable-pkg@1.0.0`, so the loop hit `continue` before ever checking the vulnerability.
2. `packageVulnerabilityAudit.isVulnerable()` is keyed by real package name, but the loop passed the manifest alias.

The manifest, or the workspace catalog when the alias comes from one, is written back at the patched version with the alias and the original pin style preserved. A selector written with a leading `=` counts as a pin too. An alias whose specifier comes from a package extension, a `readPackage` hook, or an override is still left alone with the existing warning.

The `npm:` splitting rules stay in one place. `parseBareSpecifier` already owned them, so they moved into `parseNpmAliasTarget`, which `@pnpm/resolving.npm-resolver` exports and both the resolver and the installer now call. `parseBareSpecifier` keeps its behavior.

prs.author: Ayush442842q
prs.body:
## Summary

The POSIX scripts `pn`, `pnpx`, `pnx` (in `pnpm/npm/pnpm/`) and the `pnpm` placeholder walk `$0` to find the file beside them. The walk treats only `/` as a separator, so a native Windows `$0` such as `C:\Users\me\node_modules\pnpm\pn` is taken for a bare name, prefixed with `./`, and rerooted on the working directory. The alias then either fails its regular-file guard or reaches a different `pnpm`.

This PR applies the same drive-letter / UNC-prefix gate that the `pnpm setup` writers already use (as of pnpm/pnpm#14797) to all four files. The same fix is also applied to the `@pnpm/exe` counterparts under `pnpm11/pnpm/artifacts/exe/` (the committed `pn`, `pnpx`, `pnx` scripts and the `prepare.js` generator).

Every one of the six scripts is covered by a test that runs it: each resolves a
drive-letter `$0`, a UNC `$0`, and — as the negative control for the gate — a Unix
`$0` holding a literal backslash. The fixtures name the file `sh` opens with the
backslashes themselves, which are ordinary characters in a POSIX file name, so
`$0` really is a native Windows path and the walk has to convert it to reach the
`pnpm` beside it. A further test pins the committed `@pnpm/exe` alias scripts to
what `prepare.js` writes, since an install regenerates them.

## Summary

A follow-up to pnpm/pnpm#15165, which left one case of the hoisted linker's install summary unreported. Raised there in [a review thread](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/15165#discussion_r4057419563).

When an optional dependency stops being usable between two installs, the two linkers do different things, and only one of them said so:

| | package after the second install | summary |
|:---|:---|:---|
| isolated | stays in `node_modules` | nothing, correctly |
| hoisted, before | **removed** | nothing |
| hoisted, after | removed | `- pkg 1.0.0` |

The hoisted linker takes the directory away as an orphan. The report added in pnpm/pnpm#15165 compares the lockfile the previous install left in `node_modules` against the one this install materializes, and it read **both** sides against **this** install's skip set, so a dependency this install skips vanished from both sides and the removal went unmentioned.

Each side is now read against the skip set of its own install: the previous install's, from its `.modules.yaml`, for the "before" side, and this install's for the "after" side. That distinction is what separates the two cases that look identical in a lockfile:

- skipped now, installed last time: the directory is gone, so report the removal.
- skipped both times: it was never there, so stay quiet.

## Summary

Fixes pnpm/pnpm#15111.

prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Waiting tasks of a concurrency group now take available slots in arrival order, with higher `priority` tasks going first. When workspaces use different group limits, a later task can take a free slot that earlier tasks cannot use.

The previous waiter path polled `try_lock` with exponential backoff, so a later arrival (still on a short poll) often took the freed slot. Each waiter now takes a ticket under `<stateDir>/run-slots/<group>/waiters/`. The oldest live waiter at the highest `priority` who can use a free slot takes it. A waiter whose process has ended is skipped because its lock is gone. When waiters share a pool with different group limits, a later waiter may take a higher-index slot that nobody ahead can reach. `pnpm tasks status` prints who is running and who is waiting in each group.

The wait notice names this run's place in line and who is ahead. Status rows show task names and elapsed time. Displayed names and paths are sanitized, and workspace paths cannot inject stamp metadata.

This is v12-only. `priority` is a new task setting; v11 keeps it as an unrecognized field the way it already keeps `concurrencyGroup`.

prs.title: fix(lockfile): re-resolve subtrees when a global pnpmfile exports readPackage
prs.author: Dextheking1
prs.body:
Fixes pnpm/pnpm#15136

## Problem

The global pnpmfile is excluded from `pnpmfileChecksum`, so changing or removing its `readPackage` hook could leave previously resolved lockfile subtrees untouched on the next `pnpm install`.

## Fix

The lockfile now records whether a checksum-excluded pnpmfile source supplied a `readPackage` hook. pnpm compares that state with the current hook configuration before taking frozen, fast-update, or subtree-reuse paths. A present untracked hook still forces resolution because edits to its implementation cannot be checksummed, while a stable global pnpmfile without `readPackage` can reuse the lockfile normally.

The pnpm v11 TypeScript implementation and pnpm v12 Rust implementation use the same behavior. Hook inspection failures now surface as pnpmfile errors instead of being treated as an absent hook.

## Testing

- Rust hook and lockfile merge tests: 6 passed.
- TypeScript deps-installer suite: 1,145 passed, 19 skipped.
- TypeScript hook, lockfile filesystem, merger, and pruner suites: 129 passed.
- Rust workspace check, Clippy, rustdoc, Dylint, rustfmt, TypeScript compile/lint/bundle, spelling, versioning, typos, and Taplo checks passed in the pre-push gate.

prs.title: fix(cli): load the pnpmfile for the commands that skipped it
prs.author: spencerbeggs
prs.body:
## Summary

Thirteen pnpm 12 commands never ran the `updateConfig` pnpmfile pass, so any setting a hook changes (a config-dependency plugin's catalogs, for example) was missing when they ran: `peers check`, `why`, `list`, `ll`, `licenses`, `audit`, `sbom`, `fetch`, `patch`, `patch-commit`, `patch-remove`, `approve-builds` and `runtime`.

The reported symptom is `pnpm peers check` aborting with `ERR_PNPM_CATALOG_ENTRY_NOT_FOUND_FOR_SPEC` when a linked workspace package's `peerDependencies` use a hook-provided catalog. That is the one place the check resolves a `catalog:` spec at run time, which is why the issue's other controls pass. `pnpm fetch` failed outright too, with `ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH`, once a hook's catalog reached the lockfile. The rest silently discarded whatever the hook changed.

pnpm 11 is not affected: it applies the hooks for every command in `main.ts`. The changeset targets `pacquet` only.

### Approach

prs.author: KSXGitHub
prs.body:
## Summary

Two functions took a value by reference and copied it, where every caller had just built that value and dropped it on the next line. The borrow existed only to satisfy the signature, and the callee paid for a copy nobody needed. Both now take the value, and the callers hand theirs over.

One is in the pnpm CLI and one is in pnpr, so the changes are separate commits.

### `TaskRunState::record_passed` — the task key

```rust
if !writer.completed.insert(key.clone()) { return Ok(()); }
// … write the record …
writer.completed.remove(key);   // roll the tentative insert back
```

Both call sites build the key and never read it again:

```rust
let key = TaskKey { project: node.project.clone(), task_name: node.task_name.clone() };
task_run_state.record_passed(&key, node, workspace_root);
```

A `TaskKey` owns a `PathBuf` and a `String`, so the clone is two allocations for every task a recursive run records.

Taking it by value meant moving the insert past the write, because the set had the key before there was a line to justify it. The rollback goes away with the reordering: `completed` is a dedup guard and `insert`'s return value was its only reader, so a `contains` followed by an `insert` is the one atomic step `insert` alone used to be — the writer lock is held across both halves, so nothing can interleave.

The old order also left a key recorded for a line it never wrote when the state file turned out to be unavailable, since that path returns `Ok` without rolling b

## Summary

**Problem.** The root project's `preinstall` runs after the dependencies are resolved and linked, together with its `install` and `postinstall`. A guard such as `npx only-allow yarn` cannot stop the install: by the time it fails, `node_modules` is already populated. prs.title: fix(pacquet): avoid store link probe during version check
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Avoid probing package store linkability during `pnpm --version` and other pre-command checks that do not require store access.

Previously, `pnpm --version` triggered store path resolution, which performed a filesystem linkability probe by creating and deleting a temporary probe file (`_tmp_<pid>_<nanos>`) in the project directory. This modified the directory timestamp and caused file watchers such as Nx to detect changes during project graph computation, leading to an infinite rebuild loop.

Store directory linkability probing is now bypassed during pre-command checks and deferred until an operation actually requires store access (e.g., when switching pnpm versions or syncing package manager dependencies).

## Squash Commit Body

```text
Avoid probing store linkability in pre-command checks when no store is required.

Running commands like `pnpm --version` previously performed a filesystem linkability
probe in the current working directory to test hardlink support against pnpm home.
The temporary file creation and deletion modified directory timestamps, causing
file watchers like Nx to detect changes and enter an infinite loop.

Add `skip_store_dir_resolution` to `Config` to bypass the probe during pre-command
checks and version flag handling, resolving store directory only when switching
pnpm versions or syncing dependencies.
```

prs.title: fix(network): cap proxy connections and retry transient connection drops
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

When downloading package tarballs in parallel through an HTTP/HTTPS proxy, requests previously had no host socket cap unless an explicit per-host limit was configured. Under high `networkConcurrency` or default concurrency (16), concurrent requests could flood the proxy connection pool, leading to connection refusals (`os error 61`) and unexpected socket closures without TLS `close_notify`.

This PR aligns pnpm v12 with pnpm v11's default behavior:
1. Proxied requests route their socket limits to the proxy's origin so targets behind the same proxy share the connection cap, while targets matched by `no_proxy` bypass the proxy and connect directly.
2. The proxy origin socket limit defaults to 50 (`DEFAULT_MAX_SOCKETS`) when uncapped, matching undici / pnpm v11.
3. Sets reqwest's `pool_max_idle_per_host(50)` and a 15-second TCP keepalive so idle connections in the pool don't stall until edge proxies or servers drop them.
4. Immediately retries transient transport errors (`is_connect()` or `is_request()`, including unexpected EOF / peer closed connection) up to 2 quick retries when fetching package archives before bubbling up to the outer backoff loop.

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15280

```text

(mirroring undici and pnpm v11) to avoid exhausting proxy connection
backlogs or triggering unexpected connection resets when parallel

prs.title: fix(update): keep a range whose shape no save prefix describes
prs.author: altaywtf
prs.body:
## Problem

`pnpm update` resolves a dependency inside its declared range and then writes back a specifier of a different shape. A top-bounded range such as `<= 1.2.5` or `>=1.0.0 <1.3.0` becomes `^1.2.0`, so the next update walks past the bound the manifest set. Both stacks derive the new specifier from the old one through `calcVersionRange` / `calc_version_range`, which classifies the existing range into a save-prefix style (`^`, `~`, exact, bare version) and falls back to the default prefix for any shape it cannot classify.

Reproduced on current `main` against the fixture registry, with `@pnpm.e2e/foo` (1.0.0 to 2.0.0, 100.x, `latest` = 100.1.0) and `@pnpm.e2e/has-prerelease`. Both the TypeScript v11 CLI and the Rust v12 CLI produced the same results:

| declared | `pnpm update` | `pnpm update --latest` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<= 1.2.5` | `^1.2.0` (bug) | `^100.1.0` |
| `>=1.0.0 <1.3.0` | `^1.2.0` (bug) | `^100.1.0` |
| `=1.1.0` | `=1.1.0` | `=100.1.0` |
| `~1.1.0` | `~1.1.0` | `~100.1.0` |
| `^3.0.0-rc.0` | `^3.0.0-rc.1` | `^3.0.0-rc.1` |
| `1.1.0` | `1.1.0` | `100.1.0` |
| `*` | `^100.1.0` | `^100.1.0` |

The `=` and prerelease-caret cases from the issue thread are already preserved on `main`; only the shapes no save prefix describes still lose their bounds.

## Summary

On Unix, calling chmod on a file owned by another user fails with EPERM even when the mode is unchanged. When package files are owned by root or another user, linking executables failed on targets that already had executable permissions.

prs.title: fix(run): stop nested scripts from duplicating PATH entries
prs.author: altaywtf
prs.body:
## Summary

A script that runs `pnpm run` inherits the `PATH` its parent script got, and `extendPath` prepends the same `node_modules/.bin`, `node-gyp-bin`, and extra bin entries on top of it again. `PATH` grows by one copy of those entries per nesting level.

`extendPath` (v11, `pnpm11/exec/npm-lifecycle`) and `extend_path` (v12, `pnpm/crates/executor`) now drop inherited `PATH` entries that exactly match an entry they prepend. Prepended entries keep their order, and every other inherited entry stays, including duplicates the user put there.

Reproduced on 11.27.1 and 12.6.0: three nested `pnpm run` levels produced three copies each of `node_modules/.bin` and `node-gyp-bin`. With this change, the local v11 bundle and v12 debug binary produce one copy of each.

Closes pnpm/pnpm#5352

## Squash Commit Body

```text
A script that runs `pnpm run` inherits the PATH its parent script got,
and extendPath prepended the same node_modules/.bin, node-gyp-bin, and
extra bin entries again on top of it, so PATH grew by one copy of them
per nesting level.

extendPath now drops inherited PATH entries that exactly match one of
the entries it prepends. The prepended entries keep their order and
priority, and every other inherited entry, including duplicates the
user put there, stays in place. The fix is applied to both the

prs.author: fengmk2
prs.body:
Registries can accept an upload before the package metadata and tarball become available. GitHub's [publish-time malware scanning announcement](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-npm-publish-time-malware-scanning-and-dual-use-metadata/) explains this delay and asks release automation to allow for it. Its [September npm publishing update](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-09-03-multiple-trusted-publishing-configurations-for-npm/) confirms that packages remain unavailable during scanning. Release workflows can therefore publish dependent packages before their dependencies become installable.

Add `pnpm publish --publish-wait-timeout <milliseconds>` to check availability before the command continues. The check requires the exact version in install metadata and an HTTP `200` response to a tarball `HEAD` request. Recursive publishing waits before it publishes dependent packages. The timeout applies per package, or per uploaded registry group with `--batch`. The `publishWaitTimeout` setting supplies a default; `0` disables the check.

prs.author: Dextheking1
prs.body:
## Bug

Warm full `pnpm dedupe` runs double-count reused packages (regression in v12): `resolved 69, reused 138` where v11 reported `resolved 69, reused 69` for the same `express@4.21.2` graph. Every reused package ID is emitted exactly twice, as seen in the issue's `found_in_store` NDJSON stream.

Root cause: `DedupeResolutionReporter::on_resolved` emits `found_in_store` during dependency resolution (after a store-index lookup), and the fetch/materialization phases then emit `found_in_store` again for the same warm package snapshots. The default reporter increments `reused` for every event without deduplicating, so each reused package counted twice.

`--lockfile-only` and `--check` runs keep the resolve-time reporting, since they run no fetch or materialization and it remains their only reuse signal.

prs.title: perf(pnpr): flush index markers with a plain fsync on Apple platforms
prs.author: EfeDurmaz16
prs.body:
## Summary

`rebuild_package_index` wrote every `.present` marker through `write_atomic`: a temp file, `sync_all`, and a rename, once per package. On Apple platforms `sync_all` is `fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)`, which also flushes the drive cache; it takes about 4 ms alone and 19 ms with twelve writers on the Blacksmith macOS runner. Every test that starts a registry over its own storage triggers a rebuild of about 270 markers, and that is where most of the macOS Rust test time went.

The markers are still published by renaming a unique temporary sibling into place, so a symlink planted at a marker path is replaced rather than followed, but the temporary file is flushed with a plain `fsync` on Apple platforms. A plain `fsync` hands the marker to the device without the drive-cache flush; the `F_FULLFSYNC` that publishes `.complete` afterwards flushes the drive cache for everything written before it, so the markers are on stable storage before `.complete` is. Linux and Windows keep `sync_all`, which is what they did before. Nothing reads the index before `.complete` exists, and a rebuild that stops early starts over on the next launch.

| main | 9,800 | 38.3 s, 39.0 s |
| this PR | 450 | 16.5 s, 11.2 s |
| `F_FULLFSYNC` made a no-op, for reference | | 8.7 s |

prs.title: fix(fs): take over a directory lock whose holder has died
prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15360. Closes pnpm/pnpm#15393, which is the same leftover lock reached through `Ctrl+C` at the `minimumReleaseAge` prompt during the switch.

When a project pins a pnpm version in `packageManager` or `devEngines`, pnpm installs that version into the package-manager store before delegating the command. That install is guarded by `DirLock`, a mkdir-style lock in `pnpm-fs`. If pnpm is killed while holding it (`Ctrl+C` during the download, say), the lock directory stays behind: the only stale detection was a 30-minute age bound, while the install callers wait 5 minutes for the lock. Every later pnpm command in the project therefore sat silently for the full 5 minutes before giving up on the lock and proceeding.

The holder of a `DirLock` now also keeps an OS file lock (`flock` / `LockFileEx`) on a held file that stands for the lock directory, for as long as it holds the lock. The OS releases that lock when the process ends, however it ends. Only the process holding the file lock creates, removes, or takes over the directory, so a waiter that gets the file lock and still finds the directory there knows its holder is gone and takes it over at once. A live holder keeps the file locked, so two running pnpm processes keep waiting for each other exactly as before.

prs.author: xiechimon
prs.body:
## Summary

A repository converted from Yarn or npm declares its workspace projects in the `workspaces` field of `package.json`, which pnpm never reads. Today pnpm warns and installs the repository as a single project, so none of the converted projects are linked.

This implements the solution suggested in pnpm/pnpm#2255 for pnpm v12 only (a new feature, so pnpm 11 is untouched). When the root manifest has a non-empty array-form `workspaces` field with at least one usable pattern and no `pnpm-workspace.yaml` exists, the install family (install, add, update, remove, dedupe, prune, deploy, unlink) creates `pnpm-workspace.yaml` with those patterns and anchors the config to it, so the projects link on the same install.

Behavior:

- An existing `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, including a symlink, is never changed or followed.

prs.author: altaywtf
prs.body:
## Summary

Removing an `overrides` entry left the version it had locked in `pnpm-lock.yaml` whenever the declared range still accepted it. The resolver reuses any locked version that satisfies a range, and the lockfile does not record which versions an override produced.

Reproduction on current main, both pnpm v11 and pnpm v12: a project depends on `semver@7.5.3` and on `make-dir@4.0.0`, which wants `semver@^7.5.3`. A fresh install gives `make-dir` semver 7.5.3. Now, when the lockfile records an unscoped override selector (no `parent>` and no `@range`) that the current `overrides` no longer have, a full resolution treats its target as if the lockfile held no version of it. An edge with no such anchor gets the highest version in range, as a fresh install would.

prs.author: zkochan
prs.body:
## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15413.

When a project pins a pnpm version or a managed runtime, pnpm installs it into a slot of the shared global virtual store under a lock. A process that found the lock held waited up to five minutes and then entered the slot without the lock. Since pnpm/pnpm#15394 a dead holder's lock is taken over at once, so a held lock is a live install, and waiting it out can take longer than installing again.

This PR makes the wait five seconds and, when it runs out, installs the engine or runtime into a private directory of the process's own under the store's `tmp/private` and runs it from there. The shared slot is never entered unlocked.

The switch and `pnpm with` paths drop it explicitly before `process::exit`, which runs no destructors.
- **`pnpm store prune` removes what a killed process, or a dispatcher that replaced itself with the runtime (unix `exec`), left behind.** Whether a private install is still in use is told by an OS file lock its handle holds on an `in-use` file inside the directory; the OS releases it when the process ends, however it ends. `prune_cas`'s tmp sweep now removes every entry of `tmp/` except the private installs sti

prs.author: zkochan

## Summary

Closes pnpm/pnpm#15439

A warm install from the store ran one rayon task per file, so every worker in the pool linked into the same package directory at once. Creating a dirent takes the parent directory's lock on every filesystem pnpm runs on, so the workers only queued on each other while the kernel spent CPU arbitrating the queue.
